messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
parts:
[moved to stan-dev --- Andrew's confusing the two lists]

We've discussed the internal vs. external specification before.
If we want to code generate based on the distinction, it's going
to have to declared ahead of time, either in the model or in
parameters passed to the code generator.

- Bob


On Jul 15, 2014, at 4:52 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:

> All the information is already in the model in the form of constraints on variables, so tagging isn't really required. The key is making the information explicitly available to the optimizer or sampler (if desired) instead of always automatically transforming things into an unconstrained space. This is basically the same plumbing that would be needed if someone wanted to implement bouncing for constrained parameters.
>
> I guess tags could be useful if someone wanted to explicitly request something be transformed to an unconstrained scale for some reason or if they explicitly wanted boundary values included/excluded.
>
>
>
>
> On Tue, Jul 15, 2014 at 4:19 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> Yup. For HMC-stan it makes sense to work on the unconstrained scale. (We’ve also talked on occasion about implementing bouncing for constrained parameters, but maybe that makes the algorithm too messy.) But for point estimation, boundary estimates come up a lot. Sometimes we go to some trouble to avoid boundary estimates (as with our boundary-avoiding priors for group-level variance parameters), other times boundary estimates are considered a plus (for example, lasso). So, indeed, maybe we should think about implementing constrained optimization in Stan. Perhaps, for example, the Stan program could be altered by including a tag for each parameter that we want to enforce will _not_ be transformed.
> A
>
>
> On Jul 15, 2014, at 10:15 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Andrew,
>>
>> NNLS is definitely using a specialized algorithm for non-negatively constrained linear least squares. See http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-negative_least_squares#Algorithms
>>
>> There are definitely things we can do about it. Simple linear bound constraints (i.e., lb <= x <= ub) are actually pretty easy to handle in optimization algorithms. The issue is the plumbing necessary to take a model and represent the constraints that way instead of how we're currently doing it with non-linear transforms. That might be worth doing as it would also allow us to play with other ways of sampling in the presence of such constraints.
>>
>> Cheers,
>> Marcus
>>
>>
>>
>>
>> On Tue, Jul 15, 2014 at 2:42 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>> Marcus:
>>
>> I agree that Stan is general so could lose to specialized least-squares programs, but it’s my impression that nnls is also a black-box program? But maybe you’re right that optimization as currently implemented in Stan will have problems with boundary estimates. That’s an interesting point, I wonder if there’s something we could do about that.
>>
>>
>>
>> On Jul 15, 2014, at 6:11 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> Hi David,
>>>
>>> The quick answer is that Stan isn't designed to solve any one specific model, it's designed to be able to work with a very general class of models. For specific models, like this one, packages which focus on solving such models are very likely to work faster. The power of Stan comes when you want to start making changes to this model to better suite your data, e.g., a student_t model, non-linear transforms of the parameters, hierarchical models, etc.
>>>
>>> This particular model may be hard for Stan because of the way constraints are handled using a log transform. This makes it effectively impossible for beta to ever be zero. If the data strongly supports that, the optimizer could end up spending a long time trying to get close to zero.
>>>
>>> Now, that said, we would like to make Stan as competitive as possible even with these simple models for which there may be specialized approaches. So, can you send along any scripts, data, initialization, etc that you were using for this so that we can look into it? Also any printed output from your Stan run would be helpful.
>>>
>>> Cheers,
>>> Marcus
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> On Mon, Jul 14, 2014 at 8:43 PM, David C Cohen <buend...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> Hi,
>>>
>>> I've been using lm (linear modeling) and nnls (nonnegative least squares) in R, and was looking for a faster alternative, and found stan. The first impression I got is that stan was not primarily designed to do the job that ln and nnls do, am I (hopefully) wrong about this?
>>>
>>> As an alternative to R's nnls, I tried the following stan model:
>>>
>>> data {
>>> int<lower=0> N; // number of data items
>>> int<lower=0> K; // number of predictors
>>> matrix[N,K] x; // predictor matrix
>>> vector[N] y; // outcome vector
>>> }
>>> parameters {
>>> vector<lower=0>[K] beta; // coefficients for predictors
>>> real<lower=0> sigma; // error scale
>>> }
>>> model {
>>> y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma); // likelihood
>>> }
>>>
>>> Using the above code in rstan, I used optimizing() function to perform the job of nnls. For N=250 and K=400, it takes 0.02 s for nnls, while the above stan equivalent takes over 3.5 s.
>>>
>>> Am I doing this wrong, or is stan not designed to solve this problem?
>>>
